newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-Belgian Mobistar sees profit by 2000.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Belgian Mobistar sees profit by 2000.

text.p: Belgian-French Mobistar NV, Belgium's second GSM mobile phone operator which was launched last August, said on Thursday it would stay deep in the red in 1997 but reach break-even by the turn of the century.
"We see in 1997 a loss which will be about the same as in 1996," Mobistar financial director Wilfried Verstraete told a news conference on 1996 results.
Mobistar had a 1996 loss of 4.19 billion francs ($118 million) which Verstraete said was entirely in line with expectations and was caused by start-up costs.
Chairman John Cordier said that according to the business plan, Mobistar would reach profit after four years. "And the way it looks now, we'll certainly achieve it," he said.

Mobistar, which was launched on August 27, now has more than 120,000 customers, up from 68,000 at the end of 1996, which was three times as many as forecast. It expects to add at least another 100,000 clients by the end of this year.
Belgium now has more than half a million GSM users, with Mobistar accounting for about a fifth.

To finance further development of the network, Mobistar raised its capital by two billion francs to 13 billion ($366 million) last week, and will sign an 18 billion franc ($507 million) 10-year financing deal with a consortium of 20 banks next week, Verstraete said.
"It's a very nice deal," said Verstraete. "We'll gradually take up the funds according to our needs," he said.
Mobistar is 57 percent owned by France Telecom. Belgian data communications company Telinfo holds 10 percent and nine other Belgian companies the balance.
Cordier, who is also Telinfo chairman, said he expected Telinfo to receive first dividends from Mobistar in 2001, one year earlier than stated by Telinfo in 1996.
Mobistar General Manager Bernard Ghillebaert said he expected global GSM market penetration in Belgium to grow to nearly eight percent this year and to 20 percent by 2000.
Turnover, which was 699 million ($19.7 million) from four months of operations in 1996, was likely to exceed four billion ($113 million) this year.
Investments, which totalled 17.6 billion francs ($496 million), including 9.0 billion ($254 million) for the licence to operate the system, would be more than five billion ($141 million) in 1997.
Belgium's first mobile service Proximus is operated by Belgacom Mobile, which is 75-percent owned by Belgian state telephone operator Belgacom and 25-percent by AirTouch Communications Inc..
Belgacom itself is 49.9 percent owned by a consortium including Ameritech, Singapore Telecom, Tele Danmark and three Belgian groups.

Ghillebaert said that following Mobistar's launch, the average monthly bill in Belgium for mobile telephone traffic had dropped to below the European average from second most expensive in Europe before the launch.

He expected a third GSM operator in Belgium next year following the liberalisation of the telecommunications market but the arrival of a new competitor was already discounted in Mobistar's earnings forecast, he said.
Cordier also said that France Telecom's France Telecom Mobiles International (FTMI) and Telinfo unit Telindus Luxembourg would bid for the second GSM licence in Luxembourg.
